extracted.intended_audience: aspiring and early-career fiction writers planning to write a novella
extracted.subtask_description: Practical craft and publication guidance for composing a novella: form-specific advice on pacing, conflict, character, structure, economy, and routes to publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flood your reading list with novellas
rubrics_metrics.description: Read many novellas first to internalize the distinctive rhythm of the form and to learn what readers expect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read with a writer's eye, not just for pleasure. While rereading classics (Animal Farm, Of Mice and Men, Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde), evaluate how they handle pace and structure. While reading, ask: Are there subplots? How many and how much space do they get? Do they involve the protagonist? Are there flashbacks/backstories and are they brief or alluded to? How long are the sentences—do they report action or are they descriptive? Consider the novella’s fast-moving pace and single-trajectory tendency; consult guides to pacing if needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nail down your central conflict
rubrics_metrics.description: Make the conflict the driving force of the novella and keep it streamlined rather than multi-layered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify a single central story thread that exerts 'gravitational pull.' Be able to summarize the central conflict in one sentence. Choose from types of conflict (seven main types exist) broadly grouped as external (e.g., protagonist vs. outside force) or internal (e.g., protagonist vs. own obsession). Streamline complexity: novellas usually cannot support overly complicated, multi-layered plots.

rubrics_metrics.name: Let your character drive the story
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the novella as a vehicle for character study; the protagonist should be the engine of action and interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sculpt the protagonist with subtlety and depth—know details about them even if they don't appear in the text. Begin with three core elements: The Goal (what the character wants), The Motivation (why they want it), and The Arc (how they change or remain the same). Favor staying in one character’s point of view throughout to allow intimacy; first-person is recommended for first-time novella writers. Consider unreliable narrators as a valid technique (e.g., The Yellow Wallpaper) to shape reader trust and perspective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep your supporting cast small and central
rubrics_metrics.description: Limit secondary characters and ensure each one serves the central plot or the protagonist’s arc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define the protagonist, then choose one or two central relationships that perform essential functions. Whenever a new character is introduced, ask whether they contribute to the central plot or the protagonist’s development; if not, cut them or amalgamate them with another character (example: merge comic-relief aunt and secret-bearing uncle into one character). Ancillary characters can be vivid but should not carry full development arcs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outline and chart narrative shape (don't write by the seat of your pants)
rubrics_metrics.description: Plan the novella’s narrative architecture before or during drafting to maximize tightness and forward momentum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clearly chart major plot points, peaks, plateaus, the ending, and milestones for roughly how long it’ll take to reach each one. Use story models as helpful templates (The Hero’s Journey, three-act structure, Dan Harmon’s story model), being mindful that novellas require tighter structure and fewer episodic detours than novels to prevent readers wondering 'where is this going?'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commit to a time and place (unity of action/time/place)
rubrics_metrics.description: Constrain the novella’s action within a limited span of time and a confined space where possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer narratives that occur over a short span—typically a few hours to a few months—and are confined to one space, following Aristotle’s unity of action, time, and place. This focus helps maintain propulsion toward a climax. If your novella does jump in time or location, indicate shifts clearly with scene breaks or white space (or use chapters if preferred) so the reader’s momentum isn’t lost.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ruthlessly revise and cut for economy
rubrics_metrics.description: Because novellas have lower word counts, every scene, sentence, and word must earn its place.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: At revision, ask for every scene: 'How does this scene further my central conflict?' or 'What have I learned that I didn’t know before?' Remove passages that don’t add. Trim subplots and fix a swollen middle. Tighten overly wordy sentences. After self-editing, work with a professional editor to refine plot progression, precision, and clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adhere to genre and market word-count expectations when aiming for traditional publication
rubrics_metrics.description: Respect genre-specific standard word counts if you plan to query agents or pursue traditional publishing, because market norms influence acquisition decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Genre and target age range determine expected length (e.g., epic fantasy tends to be longer; some nonfiction has typical lengths). Agents and publishers use word count as a filter; being far outside expectations can hinder saleability. However, there are exceptions backed by established authors or market support. If self-publishing, word count is less critical—focus on telling a good story. Research recent target ranges for your genre before querying.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose appropriate publication routes and format considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide whether to seek literary magazine placement, serialisation, an agent for book publication, or self-publishing—each has implications for length and presentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If submitting to magazines, they may publish a section of a longer novella or serialize it. For book publication, contact literary agents who can connect you with publishers; novellas are harder to place with major publishers, especially for debut authors, but independent and e-publishers may be receptive. Self-publishing is a practical alternative and can work well for novellas. Research outlet norms and target your submissions accordingly.
